extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, literary readers, and critics interested in dramatic composition and moral depiction
extracted.subtask_description: Authorial guidance on composing a dramatic narrative (a tragedy) that truthfully portrays vice and human psychology, prioritizing moral and psychological realism over strict stage rules and popular sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat play as dramatic narrative rather than strict stage piece
rubrics_metrics.description: This play is to be regarded merely as a dramatic narrative in which, for the purpose of tracing out the innermost workings of the soul, advantage has been taken of the dramatic method, without otherwise conforming to the stringent rules of theatrical composition, or seeking the dubious advantage of stage adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explicitly rejects strict adherence to classical theatrical rules and stage-adaptability when such constraints would prevent exploration of inner life; accept compressed or improbable incidents if they serve psychological revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compress incident for inner psychological development
rubrics_metrics.description: It must be admitted as somewhat inconsistent that three very remarkable people, whose acts are dependent on perhaps a thousand contingencies, should be completely developed within three hours...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges and defends crowding incidents and rapid development of character when necessary to 'trace out the innermost workings of the soul.' Improbability of temporal compression is allowable for narrative/psychological aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unveil crime fully to condemn it
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever proposes to discourage vice and to vindicate religion, morality, and social order against their enemies, must unveil crime in all its deformity; he must diligently explore its dark mazes, and make himself familiar with sentiments at the wickedness of which his soul revolts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To expose vice effectively the dramatist must portray its mechanisms and sentiments in full—even if offensive or shocking—so that its deformity is evident and serves a moral purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expose the inner workings of vice (detailed villain psychology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Vice is here exposed in its innermost workings. In Francis it resolves all the confused terrors of conscience into wild abstractions, destroys virtuous sentiments by dissecting them, and holds up the earnest voice of religion to mockery and scorn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch striking, lifelike portraits of villainy that show how the character's intellect and rationalizations operate; the machinery of vice should be held up to abhorrence by revealing its internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast vice with truth/virtue to test its strength
rubrics_metrics.description: I have endeavored to sketch a striking and lifelike portrait, to hold up to abhorrence all the machinery of his scheme of vice, and to test its strength by contrasting it with truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrast—place truth or virtue against vice—to reveal vice's deformity and to demonstrate the moral argument of the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray complex villains with redeeming intellectual qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: I have made these said immoral characters to stand out favorably in particular points, and even in some measure to compensate by qualities of the head for what they are deficient in those of the heart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give even depraved characters certain admirable qualities (intellect, energy, grandeur) so they are compelling and believable; avoid one-dimensional caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid utterly irredeemable characters as subjects for art
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who is so utterly depraved as to be without a single redeeming point is no meet subject for art, and would disgust rather than excite the interest of the reader; who would turn over with impatience the pages which concern him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters retain some redeeming or interesting traits; completely soulless villains repel the audience and fail artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke mixed responses (pity and hatred) toward great misguided souls
rubrics_metrics.description: Great and majestic in misfortune, by misfortune reclaimed, and led back to the paths of virtue. Such a man shall you pity and hate, abhor yet love, in the Robber Moor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to produce complex emotional reactions—readers/viewers should both pity and condemn the protagonist; complexity deepens moral and aesthetic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sanitize truth to please tender sensibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps, in order to please tender-hearted people, I might have been less true to nature; but ... shall therefore pearls, fire, and water be condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist altering truthful depiction of human nature and vice merely to placate delicate audiences; fidelity to nature is prioritized over immediate agreeableness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize risk of public misinterpretation and require strong-minded audience
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain strength of mind is required both on the part of the poet and the reader; in the former that he may not disguise vice, in the latter that he may not suffer brilliant qualities to beguile him into admiration of what is essentially detestable. The vulgar ... will ... pretend to discover in my work an apology for the very vice which it has been my object to condemn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that vivid depiction of vice can be misconstrued as endorsement; the author must be resolute in portrayal, and accept that some readers ('the vulgar') may miss the moral aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: End with moral retribution / didactic resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: In consequence of the remarkable catastrophe which ends my play, I may justly claim for it a place among books of morality, for crime meets at last with the punishment it deserves; the lost one enters again within the pale of the law, and virtue is triumphant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the aim is moral instruction, ensure the plot concludes with appropriate punishment or redemption so that the ethical argument is clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use drama to trace innermost workings of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of tracing out the innermost workings of the soul, advantage has been taken of the dramatic method...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ dramatic form chiefly as a means of psychological exploration; interior motivations and moral struggle are central aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject slavish observance of classical unities when limiting artistic truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A greater amount of incident is here crowded together than it was possible for me to confine within the narrow limits prescribed by Aristotle and Batteux.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not be bound by classical prescriptions (unity of time/place/action) if they impede truthful or effective portrayal of characters and moral themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance artistic fidelity and public sensibilities in later editions
rubrics_metrics.description: This second edition ... has been improved by greater care in printing, and by the omission of those equivocal sentences which were offensive to the more fastidious part of the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While initial truthfulness may be preserved, consider prudent editorial adjustments (omitting equivocals, arranging songs) to broaden accessibility without abandoning core moral intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic aim: instruct youth by showing consequences of excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the youth behold with alarm the consequences of unbridled excess; nor let the man depart without imbibing the lesson that the invisible band of Providence makes even villains the instruments of its designs and judgments...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape the narrative so that it functions pedagogically—young readers should be warned by example while adults are led to reflect on providence and moral order.
